Raising energy on model samples (the second term of Eq. 4 ) can be prohibitively expensive, and several methods approximate it with samples from short Markov chains or relaxations [ 31 , 58 , 45 ] .
In this paper, we primarily use a pseudolikelihood (PL) objective for its combination of high accuracy, simplicity, and short fitting time on these tasks [ 8 , 37 ] , though other methods are similarly effective (see Table 7 ).
See Secs. D.1 and C for training details.

We test against HRM [ 62 ] , Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) [ 38 ] , Generative Recursive Reasoning (GRAM) [ 3 ] , Equilibrium Reasoners (EqR) [ 36 ] , Flow Reasoning Models (FRM) [ 29 ] , Tiny Recursive Message Passing (TRMP) [ 52 ] and Energy Based Reasoners (EBR) [ 11 ] .
Where available, we retrain each baseline with its authors’ code and recipe on one H200 for timing and score each baseline with its published inference setting. We score every method on the same test set of each task, and no method chooses a setting or a checkpoint on the test set ( App. C.1 ). CRAM and each baseline trains with three seeds, and we report the mean over the three runs.
We compare only against models that produce the answer by their own recurrent computation.
Methods that pass learned costs to an external exact solver [ 10 , 16 , 17 ] are outside the scope of this work.

Figure 4: Local methods that avoid sampling the energy train significantly faster. We train CRAM with five objectives, the four named below and one-step BPTT [ 62 ] , and plot the mean solve rate on 512 Sudoku-Extreme development puzzles over 20 training runs against training time.
Bands span the 25th to 75th percentile of the runs.
The mean reaches 99% (circles) after 48 ms with pseudolikelihood [ 8 ] and 0.21 s with minimum probability flow [ 56 ] , against 4.4 s with one-step BPTT and 33 s with contrastive divergence [ 31 ] . Full BPTT [ 63 ] ends at a mean of 27% after 245 s, still rising at the end of its schedule; with 3,840,000 updates (about 5 h) it solves 48.8% of test puzzles.
Training times include fitting the stopping threshold from the training solutions (24–75 ms) and exclude each run’s one-time start-up (0.08–0.30 s), as do the T 99 times of Table 7 , which compares twelve methods on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique; App. D gives details of each objective.

T 99 is the median over the three runs of the fit time at the first probe where their mean reaches 99%, minus each run’s one-time start-up (0.10–1.83 s on Sudoku-Extreme and 0.64–1.22 s on Maze-Unique), plus the time to fit the stopping threshold and focus statistic (24–75 ms on Sudoku-Extreme; the Maze-Unique search fits none).

Table 7: Nine of the twelve training methods reach at least 99% test accuracy on both tasks, and a local objective is the first to reach 99% on the development probe of each task. T 99 : training time until the mean development solve rate of three runs first reaches 99% (dash: never). FLOPs 99 : training arithmetic to that point. Solved : exact test solve rate (%), mean SD over three runs. Classes, protocol and notes in App. D ; bold: best value of each column. Every method runs in one shared training harness that is slower than the recipes of Table 2 , so compare these times with each other, not with Table 2 : a full pseudolikelihood fit on Sudoku-Extreme takes about 70 ms here, against 42 ms there.
